sourceNotes: Seeded from ETDM roleplay performance indicators and entrepreneurship cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: ETDM event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the entrepreneurship cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: An early judgment about whether a product, service, or venture idea is practical enough to keep developing.
terms.whyItMatters: ETDM teams often need to show that an idea can work before recommending full implementation.

terms.definition: The identity, promise, and associations customers connect with a specific product or service.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand-building helps ETDM teams show how a new service will be remembered and trusted.

terms.definition: A comparison of the expected costs of a decision with the expected gains or advantages.
terms.whyItMatters: This gives teams a clean way to defend a recommendation beyond saying it sounds good.

terms.definition: Actions taken to reduce the likelihood or impact of an identified business risk.
terms.whyItMatters: A strong team answer does not only identify risk; it explains how the business can control it.

terms.definition: The resources, approvals, staff, systems, and funds needed before a new business or service can launch.
terms.whyItMatters: Helps teams organize implementation details in venture-planning cases.

terms.definition: Planning resources such as business plans, budgets, forecasts, timelines, and feasibility checklists.
terms.whyItMatters: These tools help entrepreneurs test assumptions before spending resources.

terms.definition: Using service quality to shape how customers view a business compared with alternatives.
terms.whyItMatters: Many ETDM cases ask teams to improve the customer experience while strengthening brand image.

terms.definition: A communication path where customers, community members, or influencers spread opinions and recommendations.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth can be especially powerful for small ventures with limited promotion budgets.

terms.definition: Reviewing applications, resumes, or qualifications to decide which candidates should move forward.
terms.whyItMatters: Screening is a basic HR process for staffing a growing entrepreneurial venture.

terms.definition: Evaluating how well employees perform assigned work and meet business expectations.
terms.whyItMatters: Teams can use this term when discussing training, service consistency, and accountability.

terms.definition: Exploring ideas and opportunities to determine whether they could become viable ventures.
terms.whyItMatters: Discovery helps entrepreneurs avoid launching ideas without customer or market evidence.

terms.definition: The effect small firms have on jobs, innovation, competition, communities, and market economies.
terms.whyItMatters: This term supports broader economic reasoning in entrepreneurship cases.

terms.definition: The revenue figure a franchise percentage is actually charged against — normally gross sales before discounts, comps, coupons and employee meals are deducted, so 6% on $800,000 of gross sales costs $48,000 whether or not the unit turned a profit.
terms.whyItMatters: An ETDM case that hands the team a franchise P&L is testing whether they compute royalties off gross sales rather than net income; a judge asking 'what does the franchisor get in a bad year?' wants the fixed dollar answer.

terms.definition: A contractual floor a licensee owes regardless of sales, so the payment is the greater of the running rate times net sales or the floor — a 5% rate against a $50,000 minimum means every year below $1,000,000 in sales is paid at the floor.
terms.whyItMatters: Licensing cases ask the team to say at what sales volume the minimum stops binding; the answer is floor divided by rate, and teams that only multiply the rate miss the downside risk the licensor built in.

terms.definition: Each outcome's payoff weighted by its probability and summed, which lets a 40% shot at $1,000,000 be compared directly against a certain $150,000 — $400,000 versus $150,000 — and turns a gut call about risk into arithmetic.
terms.whyItMatters: Team decision cases that supply probabilities for a product launch expect the weighted figure and an explicit note that the team can survive the losing branch, not just the biggest number.

terms.definition: The volume at which two cost structures cost exactly the same, found by dividing the difference in fixed costs by the difference in variable costs per unit; below it the low-fixed-cost option wins, above it the capital-intensive one does.
terms.whyItMatters: Make-or-buy and in-house-versus-contract-manufacturer cases are graded on the crossover volume and where the forecast sits relative to it, not on a preference for owning equipment.

terms.definition: The sales level at which a retail tenant starts owing percentage rent, computed as base rent divided by the percentage rate — $120,000 of base rent at 6% means overage rent begins only above $2,000,000 in sales.
terms.whyItMatters: Mall-lease negotiation roleplays are won by computing the breakpoint from the offered base rent and showing the projected sales fall under it, so the percentage clause costs the venture nothing.

terms.definition: A present-value comparison that sets the after-tax cost of the lease stream against the purchase price less the discounted salvage value plus the tax shield from depreciation, so the cheaper monthly payment can still lose on total cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Equipment and facility cases hand the team a monthly lease quote and a purchase price; the recommendation must rest on discounted totals and residual value, since judges probe for the salvage assumption.

terms.definition: Net operating income divided by property value, which inverts to price a building the venture might buy instead of lease — $90,000 of net operating income at an 8% market rate implies $1,125,000, and a lower rate implies a higher price for identical income.
terms.whyItMatters: Cases where the founder can purchase the building rather than renew the lease turn on this conversion; it is also how the team values the real estate separately from the operating business at exit.

terms.definition: Net profit added back to one working owner's compensation, personal perks, interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization — the benefit stream a small owner-operated business is priced on, typically at two to three times, where larger deals switch to a multiple of EBITDA.
terms.whyItMatters: Buy-an-existing-business cases give a tax return showing thin profit; the team must recast it into the owner benefit stream before applying a multiple, or it will value a healthy business at nearly nothing.

terms.definition: Working backward from an assumed exit: divide the projected sale value by the investor's target return to get today's post-money figure, then divide the check by that figure for the ownership demanded — a $30,000,000 exit at a 10x target supports a $3,000,000 valuation, so $600,000 buys 20%.
terms.whyItMatters: Pitch-and-negotiate cases give an exit assumption and a required return; the team that runs the chain gets a defensible ownership number instead of arguing about what the idea feels worth.

terms.definition: The normalized level of receivables plus inventory less payables a buyer requires the business to carry at closing; delivering below it cuts the purchase price dollar for dollar, so a seller who collects hard and stops reordering before the sale simply pays the money back.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-acquisition cases where the seller drains cash before closing test whether the team protects the buyer with a peg and a true-up rather than trusting the headline price.

terms.definition: A per-owner running balance of contributions plus allocated profits minus draws and losses; on dissolution the assets are distributed by these ending balances, not by the profit-sharing percentages, so a partner who drew heavily can walk away with far less than their stated share.
terms.whyItMatters: Partner-dispute roleplays where two 50/50 owners contributed unequal cash are decided by these balances, and a team that answers 'they split it evenly' has misread the agreement.

terms.definition: Letting a licensee put a trademark on goods without policing their quality, which courts treat as abandonment — the owner can lose the mark outright even though every royalty check cleared on time.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand-licensing cases where the founder wants passive income test whether the team writes in sample approval and inspection rights; the risk being graded is loss of the mark, not lost royalties.

terms.definition: Rent plus common area charges, taxes and insurance divided by store sales; retail concepts fail above roughly 10% and full-service restaurants above about 8%, so the percentage, not the monthly dollar figure, says whether a space is affordable.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection cases supply a rent quote and a sales forecast; the team must convert them into this percentage and reject spaces over the benchmark even when the rent looks cheap in isolation.

terms.definition: The gap between usable and rentable square feet, expressed as a multiplier for the tenant's share of lobbies and corridors: 1,000 usable feet at a 15% factor is billed as 1,176 rentable feet every month.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two space quotes per square foot means nothing until both are restated on the same basis, and cases include the factor precisely to see which team divides it back out.

terms.definition: The full obligation over the term spread across every month of it, so twelve months free on a sixty-month term quoted at $5,000 is truly $4,000 — concessions are a discount on the average, not free money.
terms.whyItMatters: Cases offering competing concession packages are graded on this one comparable figure; a team quoting only the face rate cannot say which landlord actually offered less.

terms.definition: Spreads one-time mold, die or fixture cost across the units it will produce, so a $40,000 tool adds $8 to each of 5,000 units but only $0.80 across 50,000 — volume, not the quote, sets the real unit cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Make-versus-outsource cases include a tooling charge the team must convert to a per-unit figure at the forecast volume before comparing suppliers or setting a price floor.

terms.definition: Cost of goods sold plus total labor including payroll taxes and benefits, tracked as a percentage of sales; a full-service restaurant that lets the combined figure pass about 65% cannot cover rent and overhead however busy it looks.
terms.whyItMatters: Food-service feasibility cases supply food, beverage and payroll lines separately, and the team that sums them against sales diagnoses the failing unit while one reading only food cost misses it.

terms.definition: The market wage a working founder gave up, charged against the venture before anyone calls it profitable — $50,000 of accounting profit earned by someone who left a $70,000 job is a $20,000 economic loss.
terms.whyItMatters: Go/no-go cases love a pro forma showing thin profit, and the team that subtracts what the founders could earn elsewhere reaches the defensible recommendation judges ask for by name.

terms.definition: Annual pre-tax cash flow divided by the cash the owners actually injected, so $36,000 of flow on $150,000 put in is 24% even when the project cost $500,000; borrowing changes it, total project return does not.
terms.whyItMatters: Acquisition and build-out cases ask which deal to fund with limited founder cash, and this ranks them on money genuinely at risk rather than on total capital deployed.

terms.definition: Buyer and seller must file the same split of the price across asset classes — equipment, inventory, non-compete, goodwill — because the mix decides the seller's tax rate and how fast the buyer can write the cost off.
terms.whyItMatters: Deal-structure roleplays where both sides already agree on price turn on this schedule, and a team treating it as paperwork hands real money to the other side.

terms.definition: A minimum claim threshold before a seller owes anything: a deductible basket pays only the excess above it while a tipping basket pays from the first dollar once crossed — near-identical wording, very different money on a $250,000 claim.
terms.whyItMatters: Deal-terms roleplays put both basket types side by side to see whether the team can price the difference instead of nodding along at either.

terms.definition: Doctrine letting creditors, tax authorities or injured customers pursue the buyer of a business's assets anyway — through de facto merger, continuity of the enterprise or unpaid sales tax — despite contract language transferring only listed obligations.
terms.whyItMatters: Buy-the-business cases treat an asset purchase as a clean slate, and the team ordering lien searches and tax clearance certificates first is the one answering the risk question judges actually ask.

terms.definition: Seller financing on which the buyer pays nothing — sometimes not even interest — for a set period, which is the condition for a lender to count it toward the buyer's required contribution; a note with current payments does not qualify.
terms.whyItMatters: Acquisition-financing cases where the buyer is short of cash are solved by structuring part of the price this way, and judges ask whether the note is genuinely on full standby.

terms.definition: The share of total project cost a buyer must put in as cash for a government-guaranteed business acquisition loan — 10% of the project, of which no more than half may come from a fully standby seller note.
terms.whyItMatters: Financing cases give a purchase price and the founders' savings, and the team must show the cash gap in dollars and close it with a compliant structure rather than assuming the lender funds everything.

terms.definition: When a partner withdraws from an at-will partnership without dissolving it, the statutory price owed is the greater of liquidation value and going-concern value of that share, with interest running from the departure date.
terms.whyItMatters: Cases where one partner quits mid-year test whether the team knows the firm continues and owes a computed buyout, rather than assuming the whole business must be sold and split.

terms.definition: Moves a new product through fixed stages separated by go/kill reviews with written criteria, so a project can die at any gate -- screening, business analysis, development, testing, launch; the long-standing planning ratio is roughly 7 serious ideas entering for every 1 commercial success.
terms.whyItMatters: Development roleplays ask what happens between an idea and a launch; the scoring point is that each gate can kill the project, not that the stages happen in order.

terms.definition: One brand's sales to a single customer divided by that customer's total category spending over the same period — a household that spends $400 a year on coffee and $120 of it at one chain gives that chain 30% — so it is a per-customer ratio, unlike market share, which divides a brand's sales by the whole category's sales across all buyers; a brand can hold flat market share while its wallet share collapses.
terms.whyItMatters: Customer-relations roleplays that ask how to grow revenue without new customers are answered with this ratio and the cross-sell that raises it.

terms.definition: The blend of advertising, publicity, sales promotion, and personal selling.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix lets competitors recommend more than one communication path.

terms.definition: (Range maximum minus range minimum) divided by the minimum, times 100 — a grade running $40,000 to $60,000 has a 50% spread. Spreads widen as jobs get bigger: roughly 30 to 40% for clerical grades, 40 to 50% for professionals and 50% or more for executives, because senior jobs give a long-tenured performer more room to grow in pay without a promotion.
terms.whyItMatters: Structuring a pay grade in a compensation roleplay requires setting the minimum and maximum from the midpoint and the intended spread, a calculation judges look for explicitly.

terms.definition: The exchange of goods, services, and capital across national borders.
terms.whyItMatters: A PI targets small-business opportunity in tariffs, logistics, and culture abroad.

terms.definition: The principle that a court follows the reasoning of earlier decisions on the same question, which is what makes American case law predictable enough to plan around. Precedent from a higher court in the same jurisdiction binds; decisions from other jurisdictions are only persuasive; and a court may distinguish a case on its facts or, rarely, overrule its own prior holding.
terms.whyItMatters: Sources-of-law exam items ask why a state trial court must follow its own supreme court but may ignore another state's.

terms.definition: Portable, shorter-lived business goods bought routinely by middle managers and written off over a few years -- hand tools, laptops, forklifts; an installation is the major capital asset such as a plant or a production line, approved by top management on a multi-year capital budget.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business selling roleplays are scored on calling on the right buyer: the pair differs by who signs, so pitching an installation to a department manager is a scoring miss.

terms.definition: A philosophy that focuses all business activities on satisfying customer needs profitably.
terms.whyItMatters: It reminds competitors that every tactic should trace back to a real customer need.

terms.definition: Rating points counted only against the demographic actually being bought instead of against every household in the market, so a broad-appeal buy delivering 200 gross rating points may deliver just 60 of these if only 30% of its viewers fall inside the target.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows a schedule looking strong on total weight but thin on the buying demographic is testing this distinction, and a media-plan roleplay that quotes only the gross figure to a client buying an 18-to-34 audience has hidden the waste.

terms.definition: Pay left above the maximum of an employee's grade after a job is re-evaluated downward or a range is lowered — the salary is frozen or paid out as a lump sum instead of a base increase until the range catches up. Its opposite, a green-circled rate, sits below the grade minimum and is corrected by moving the employee up to at least the minimum, usually on a set schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: In a restructuring roleplay you must say what happens to a person whose job was downgraded; freezing base pay rather than cutting it is the answer judges expect.

terms.definition: Lifetime gross profit expected from a customer divided by the cost of winning that customer. Investors treat 3:1 as the working floor for a fundable venture; below 1:1 the business is buying revenue at a loss, and above roughly 5:1 the usual reading is underinvestment in growth rather than excellence.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship exam question hands you a lifetime value and an acquisition cost and asks whether to scale spending; the benchmark number is the tested content, and the ratio must use gross profit, not revenue.

terms.definition: The reasoning error of treating sequence as cause: sales rose after the new sign went up, therefore the sign raised sales. The test has two parts - could any other change explain the same movement (season, a competitor closing, a price cut, a general market lift), and is there a mechanism connecting the two? It is the fallacy behind most claimed advertising results, because campaigns are launched in the same weeks that demand naturally climbs.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay that hands you a sales bump right after a campaign is scored on whether you ask for a control comparison instead of claiming the credit.

terms.definition: Applies stated go/no-go criteria to drop weak concepts before money is spent, and guards against two opposite errors -- a drop-error that kills a winner and a go-error that carries a loser into costly development; idea generation, by contrast, deliberately withholds all judgment to maximize the count.
terms.whyItMatters: A brainstorming roleplay is scored badly if you evaluate while generating; competitors must say which stage they are in and which error that stage is trying to avoid.

terms.definition: The percentage of a category's national sales occurring in one market divided by the percentage of the national population living there, multiplied by 100 — a metro holding 2% of the population but 3% of category sales scores 150 — where 100 is exactly average and anything above it means the category is over-developed in that market regardless of how any single brand performs there.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-allocation roleplays ask which markets deserve the spend; the index pair, not gut feel about city size, is what a judge expects to hear.

terms.definition: Paid, nonpersonal communication delivered through media to large audiences.
terms.whyItMatters: Advertising builds broad brand awareness efficiently and at scale.

terms.definition: Non-wage offerings such as health insurance, retirement plans, and paid time off.
terms.whyItMatters: Benefits influence hiring decisions and employee satisfaction.

terms.definition: An individual who funds an early-stage startup in exchange for equity.
terms.whyItMatters: Angels are a realistic funding source competitors weigh against loans or savings.

terms.definition: Any gap between what the customer expected and what was delivered, including delivery that met every internal specification — a technically perfect order arriving after a promised time has failed. A defect is a measurable breach of a standard the company set, so every defect is a failure while many failures pass every internal check, which is why complaint data can never be replaced by quality-control data.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the operation insists nothing went wrong is won by naming this distinction before proposing the remedy.

terms.definition: A finished business good that goes into another product and keeps its own identity there -- a car battery, a tire, a microchip; raw materials are processed until that identity is lost, and maintenance and repair supplies never enter the finished product at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Industrial product questions ask you to classify an input; the identity test decides it, and it also explains why component makers can advertise to the end consumer at all.

terms.definition: The bundle of benefits a business promises to deliver to a specific customer group.
terms.whyItMatters: A sharp value proposition anchors positioning, messaging, and pricing.

terms.definition: One percent of all the households or people in a market's universe, counted whether or not their set is switched on, so a program watched by 90,000 homes in a 1,500,000-household market rates 6.0.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost-per-point math on the marketing exam starts here, and competitors lose the item by treating the figure as a share of viewers rather than a percent of the whole market.

terms.definition: The differential between a long-tenured employee and a newly hired peer shrinking to nothing or inverting — a five-year employee at $58,000 next to a new hire brought in at $61,000 because market rates rose faster than annual merit increases of 3%. It differs from a straight pay-equity gap in that the cause is market movement over time rather than a protected characteristic, and the fix is a market adjustment, not a discrimination remedy.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay in which top performers resign after a hiring spree is usually a compression problem, and naming the differential is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Revenue from one starting cohort measured a year later — upgrades and expansion added, downgrades and cancellations subtracted — divided by what that cohort paid at the start. It can exceed 100% when existing customers grow, whereas gross revenue retention counts only losses and can therefore never pass 100%.
terms.whyItMatters: In a roleplay defending a growth forecast, this figure is the evidence that revenue compounds without new customers; quoting the gross figure instead understates the venture and the judge will catch the cap at 100%.

terms.definition: The ability to produce a good at a lower OPPORTUNITY cost than a trading partner, which is what makes trade mutually profitable even when one country is more efficient at producing everything. Absolute advantage — simply making more per hour of input — does not by itself establish any reason to trade.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade items give a two-country, two-good output table and ask who should specialize in what; the answer comes from the opportunity-cost ratios, not from whichever column of raw output is larger.

terms.definition: Places a pre-release version with outside customers doing real work in their own conditions, capturing failures no internal lab reproduces; alpha testing comes first and is run in-house by employees, so a beta's whole value is the uncontrolled use an alpha deliberately excludes.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a limited launch is scored on why outside users are needed before full production, not merely on saying the product will be tested.

terms.definition: The percentage of one brand's national sales made in a market divided by that market's percentage of national population, times 100; read against the category index it sorts markets into four actions — high BDI with low CDI means a strong brand in a weak category, while low BDI with high CDI is the classic opportunity market where the category sells well and the brand does not, and both indexes below 100 argues for withdrawal.
terms.whyItMatters: The paired index read is the standard answer to a roleplay asking which market to defend and which to invest in; giving one index without the other gets a follow-up you cannot answer.

terms.definition: Short-term incentives like coupons, contests, and discounts that spur purchases.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotions drive quick sales, trial, and inventory clearance.

terms.definition: Including people of different backgrounds, perspectives, and identities in the workforce.
terms.whyItMatters: Diversity improves problem-solving and reflects the customer base.

terms.definition: Profit or loss on one customer or one order taken alone — price minus the variable cost of delivering it, measured before any fixed overhead is spread. A venture can report a healthy blended gross margin and still lose money on every additional unit once shipping, payment fees and support are charged against that unit.
terms.whyItMatters: In a growth roleplay the judge asks whether to spend more on customer acquisition; the correct answer is conditional on this figure being positive, because scaling a negative one accelerates the losses.

terms.definition: Overestimating both the intensity and the duration of a future emotional reaction; the duration half alone is the durability bias, and the two named causes are focalism -- attending only to the focal event and not to everything else that will fill the day -- and immune neglect, discounting how quickly one rationalizes an outcome. Lottery winners and people newly paralyzed converge far closer than either group predicts.
terms.whyItMatters: A risk-of-personal-decisions item asking whether a competitor should take a demanding promotion is testing this: the answer that survives is one that weighs the ordinary days after the change, not the peak of the reaction to it.

terms.definition: The contract section fixing measurable performance targets and the credit owed when they are missed: 99.9% monthly uptime allows roughly 43 minutes of outage in a 30-day month, and each tier missed below that refunds a stated percentage of the month's fee.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-services roleplays ask what the client is actually promised; converting a percentage into allowed minutes and naming the credit is what makes the promise enforceable.

terms.definition: Distinct customers who bought at least once in a period divided by the total defined target population, as a percentage — 40,000 buyers out of a 500,000-person target is 8% — which counts buyers, not units or dollars; that is exactly what separates it from market share, so a brand can raise share by selling more to the same people while its penetration does not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Growth roleplays hinge on whether the plan should recruit new buyers or sell more to current ones, and this is the number that tells the judge you know which lever you chose.

terms.definition: The percentage of sets actually in use that are tuned to a given program, so a show rating 6 in a market where only half the sets are on carries a 12 — the figure is always larger than the program's own rating because its denominator is smaller.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a rating and this figure for the same program and ask which one a national advertiser should buy against; the answer is the rating, because only it is measured against the full market a campaign is paying to cover.

terms.definition: A grid whose rows are performance ratings and whose columns are quartiles of the pay range, with a percentage in each cell: an outstanding performer in the first quartile might receive 6% while the same rating in the fourth quartile receives 3%, and a below-standard rating receives 0% anywhere. The two-way design keeps high performers moving toward the midpoint while stopping anyone from being pushed past the maximum.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a rating and a compa-ratio in a roleplay, you are expected to read the correct cell and explain why two people with the same rating get different percentages.

terms.definition: Share of customer accounts lost during a period, counted one per account no matter how large. Revenue churn instead weights every loss by the dollars it carried, so a venture that loses ten tiny accounts while keeping one enormous one shows alarming account churn alongside near-zero revenue churn.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay presents both numbers and asks which crisis to work on; the judge is testing whether you can say which measure the customer-concentration risk actually shows up in.

terms.definition: A deposit locked for a fixed term at a fixed rate, paying more than a savings account in exchange for a penalty on early withdrawal.
terms.whyItMatters: Savings-vehicle scenarios rule it out for an emergency fund precisely because the money is not reachable without giving up interest.

terms.definition: Scores quality as perception minus expectation on paired 22-item scales across five dimensions -- reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy, responsiveness -- so a dimension scoring 0 means expectations were met exactly and every negative number is a measured shortfall to fix.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how you would measure service quality is scored on the subtraction: measuring satisfaction alone cannot tell an over-promise from an under-delivery.

terms.definition: The core marketing activities such as pricing, promotion, selling, and distribution.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors organize their analysis around which marketing functions a decision touches.

terms.definition: Direct, person-to-person communication to inform, persuade, and build relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: It enables customized pitches and problem-solving for high-value sales.

terms.definition: Employer benefit and payroll-tax cost expressed as a percentage of base pay — $19,500 of insurance, retirement and taxes on a $65,000 salary is a 30% load, making the fully loaded cost $84,500. National figures put benefits near 31% of total compensation, which is why an offer decision compares loaded cost rather than salary alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Budgeting a new position in a roleplay is wrong if you quote only the salary; judges look for the loaded figure when the owner asks what the hire really costs.

terms.definition: The state in which demand pulls harder than the sales effort pushes, and it is measured rather than felt: the Sean Ellis survey treats it as reached when more than 40% of active users say they would be very disappointed if the product disappeared, alongside flattening retention curves.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a roleplay when the venture should hire salespeople, the graded answer is not yet if the threshold is unmet — hiring ahead of it burns the runway on a product customers do not miss.

terms.definition: Standards governing the responsible collection, use, protection, and sharing of information.
terms.whyItMatters: Privacy and data-governance dilemmas are common in modern business scenarios.

terms.definition: Sells the finished product with its full marketing plan in a few representative cities while matched control cities keep the old plan, so the result read is the difference between the two areas rather than the test area's raw sales; the cost is secrecy, since rivals see the plan months early.
terms.whyItMatters: Launch roleplays ask how you would prove the plan works before national rollout; the matched control is the detail that turns a demo into a measurement.

terms.definition: The top rung of the three-stage loyalty ladder: at recognition the buyer merely knows the mark, at preference the buyer chooses it but accepts a substitute when it is out of stock, and at insistence the buyer will leave the store or delay the purchase rather than take another brand — the only stage that lets a firm hold price through a competitor's promotion.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask what a strong brand is actually worth; naming the three stages and the out-of-stock behavior that separates preference from insistence is what earns the point.

terms.definition: The number of exposures needed inside a single purchase cycle before a message registers at all — below it the spend is wasted and above it the spend is redundant. The working planning standard is three exposures, from Krugman's three-hit theory.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a client wants the budget spread over more vehicles is a test of this: adding vehicles raises reach but can drop everyone below three exposures, leaving a campaign that technically touched the market and communicated nothing.

terms.definition: Managing the relationship between employers and employees, including unions and disputes.
terms.whyItMatters: Effective labor relations minimize conflict and keep the workforce productive.

terms.definition: The short summary of an investment's price, preference and control terms that precedes the definitive documents. Almost all of it is expressly non-binding — only the no-shop exclusivity clause and the confidentiality clause bind on signature — which is why a signed one still lets either side walk away over valuation.
terms.whyItMatters: In a financing roleplay a competitor who calls this a signed deal loses the point; the judge wants to hear which two clauses actually bind and that exclusivity stops you shopping the offer elsewhere.

terms.definition: Inspecting a randomly drawn sample from a delivered lot and accepting or rejecting the entire lot on the count of defects found, against a stated acceptable quality level — the highest defect percentage treated as satisfactory — which trades a known risk of passing a bad lot for the cost of inspecting every unit.
terms.whyItMatters: Receiving-process questions ask how a buyer verifies a large shipment economically; naming the tolerable defect percentage and the risk it accepts is what distinguishes a full answer from 'check some of them'.

terms.definition: Locates a failure in one of five gaps -- not knowing what customers expect, setting wrong standards, delivery that misses those standards, promotion promising what operations cannot deliver, and the customer gap between expectation and perception, which is produced by the first four.
terms.whyItMatters: Guest-recovery roleplays are scored on diagnosing which gap caused the complaint, since an over-promising ad and an untrained server call for opposite fixes.

terms.definition: The added value a strong, well-known brand name gives a product.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand equity explains why customers pay more for, and stay loyal to, established brands.

terms.definition: Activities that build positive relationships with the public and media.
terms.whyItMatters: PR manages image, trust, and credibility through third-party voices.

terms.definition: A premium paid for working a less desirable schedule, set either as cents per hour or as a percentage — commonly 10% for evenings and 15% for nights, so $20.00 an hour becomes $23.00 on nights. It is not overtime: it is owed for the hours themselves regardless of weekly total, and it must be folded into the regular rate before time-and-a-half is computed, so the overtime hour is $34.50, not $30.00.
terms.whyItMatters: Payroll questions test whether the differential enters the regular rate before the overtime multiplier, a step candidates routinely skip.

terms.definition: Annual revenue if every possible buyer bought — market units times average selling price, or the bottom-up count of buyers times price per buyer. The serviceable addressable slice is only the portion the venture's model, licensing and geography can reach, and the serviceable obtainable slice is the share it could realistically win within a few years.
terms.whyItMatters: A venture-pitch roleplay is scored partly on whether the market figure was built up from buyers and prices or borrowed from a headline industry number; the three-tier breakdown is what makes it defensible.

terms.definition: FINRA registration permitting an individual to sell general securities to the public, earned by passing the Securities Industry Essentials exam plus a top-off exam and requiring sponsorship by a member firm — a candidate cannot even sit for it unaffiliated. Charging a fee for advice rather than selling products requires a Series 65 or 66 instead.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services roleplay that asks what a new advisor may do on day one hinges on which registration is in place and who sponsored it.

terms.definition: Something buyers do not think to look for and may not know exists, so it has to be sold to them rather than bought -- burial plots, life insurance, a brand-new category's first entrant; a specialty good is the opposite pole, actively hunted by name with special effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling roleplays for insurance or services are scored on recognizing that no one walks in asking, which forces prospecting and personal selling rather than displays.

terms.definition: Attributes a brand must match well enough for buyers to accept it as a legitimate member of the category — a car that is safe, a bank that clears deposits — which buy entry and win no preference at all; the attributes that win preference are points of difference, and because parity is a threshold rather than a scale, money spent beating a rival on a parity attribute returns nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking where to invest a product-improvement budget is a parity-versus-difference question; spending to over-deliver on a category minimum is the error the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: The share of the target exposed at or above the threshold number of times — conventionally three or more — so a schedule with 70% total reach may deliver only 35% of this, because the half of the audience that saw the ad once or twice does not count toward it.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-plan items give a reach curve and a frequency distribution and ask which of two schedules performs better; the one with lower total reach usually wins because more of its audience cleared the three-exposure threshold.

terms.definition: An employer contribution formula that exempts a retirement plan from annual nondiscrimination testing: the basic version matches 100% of the first 3% of pay an employee defers plus 50% of the next 2%, capping the employer at 4% of pay, and the alternative is a 3% nonelective contribution to every eligible employee whether they defer or not. Safe harbor money must be fully vested immediately, unlike a discretionary match.
terms.whyItMatters: A benefits roleplay for a small business with highly paid owners turns on the safe harbor as the way to let owners defer fully, and the judge expects the formula.

terms.definition: The first priced round of preferred stock — commonly $5 million to $20 million for 15% to 25% of the company — raised on evidence that revenue repeats predictably. A seed round is smaller, frequently sold on a note or SAFE with no set price, and pays for the search for that repeatability rather than for scaling it.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a financing roleplay which round the venture is ready for, the graded answer is a milestone claim, not a dollar amount: repeatable revenue first, then the priced round.

terms.definition: A defect-reduction discipline targeting no more than 3.4 defects per million opportunities, executed through the DMAIC sequence — define, measure, analyze, improve, control — with trained belt roles owning each project; it attacks process variation, while lean methods attack waste and cycle time.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations-management exam items name the improvement sequence and expect the letters of DMAIC in order along with the defect target.

terms.definition: The band between desired service, what the customer hopes for, and adequate service, the least they will accept: performance inside the band passes unnoticed, above it delights, below it triggers complaint or defection, and the band narrows sharply in urgent or first-time-fix situations.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about exceeding guest expectations are scored on knowing that ordinary delivery earns nothing; the band explains why effort spent in the middle is invisible.

terms.definition: Attributes buyers strongly associate with one brand, rate favorably, and believe no competitor delivers as well — all three conditions, not just the first — which is what makes them the reason to choose it, unlike points of parity, which only qualify the brand for the consideration set; once rivals match a claimed difference it has quietly become a parity attribute and stops moving share even though the advertising still runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to identify what sets a company apart, a competitor who names a feature every rival also offers has named a parity attribute and will be corrected on the spot.

terms.definition: Unpaid media coverage generated through PR, news, and referrals.
terms.whyItMatters: Publicity builds credibility through sources other than paid ads.

terms.definition: Analyzing the current workforce and forecasting future talent needs.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures a business has the right people and skills to meet its goals.

terms.definition: The preferred holder's first claim on exit proceeds, normally 1x the money invested before common stock receives anything. Non-participating means the holder chooses the preference or converts to common, whichever pays more; participating means the holder takes the preference and then shares the remainder alongside common.
terms.whyItMatters: An exit roleplay gives a sale price below the last valuation and asks what the founders receive; the participating-versus-non-participating split changes that answer entirely and is the graded distinction.

terms.definition: An independent salesperson carrying several producers' NON-COMPETING lines in a defined territory on commission of roughly 5 to 15 percent of net sales, with no title to the goods and no authority to set price or terms. A selling agent is the stronger form: it contracts for a producer's ENTIRE output and does hold authority over price, terms and promotion, effectively acting as that producer's marketing department.
terms.whyItMatters: A start-up roleplay choosing between hiring salespeople and appointing reps is graded on the fixed-versus-variable cost trade and on who controls pricing under each arrangement.

terms.definition: A tangible item expected to survive repeated use, the standard statistical cutoff being an expected life of three years or more, which is why appliances and vehicles qualify; nondurables are consumed in one or a few uses and are bought on habit rather than deliberation.
terms.whyItMatters: Warranty, financing, and personal-selling effort all follow this split, so an exam item on why one product gets a service plan and another does not is answered with the three-year line.

terms.definition: The percentage of total sales in a market captured by one business or product.
terms.whyItMatters: Market share quantifies competitive position and the payoff of a growth strategy.

terms.definition: A schedule carrying a low continuous weight all year with heavier bursts layered over the peak selling weeks, so unlike flighting the brand is never entirely off air, and unlike continuity the weekly weight is not flat.
terms.whyItMatters: A client with year-round sales and a holiday spike is the standard prompt for this pattern; naming it and drawing the line against the other two schedules is what separates a scored answer from a vague one.

terms.definition: Ownership of employer retirement contributions earned in slices — commonly 20% after two years of service and 20% each year thereafter, reaching 100% at six years, so an employee leaving at year four keeps 60%. The alternative, cliff vesting, gives 0% until a single date and 100% on it, capped by law at three years for defined contribution plans; employee deferrals are always 100% vested from the first dollar under either schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a roleplay what a departing employee takes with them, you must apply the schedule to the years of service instead of assuming the whole account balance.

terms.definition: A single-page grid of nine blocks — customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships and cost structure — used in place of a long written plan so that assumptions about how money is made can be swapped and retested quickly.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks you to lay out a venture in ten minutes, working the nine blocks aloud gives the judge a complete answer; the two right-hand-side blocks people forget are key partnerships and cost structure.

terms.definition: The specific customer group a business chooses as its primary marketing audience.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommendations are stronger when they name a specific audience.

terms.definition: The severest federal recall classification, used when a defect carries a reasonable probability of serious injury or death; Class II covers defects whose harm is temporary or medically reversible and where serious harm is remote, and Class III covers violations unlikely to cause any harm.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-protection questions give a defect scenario and ask how urgently the firm must act; the class decides the notification reach and the speed regulators expect.

terms.definition: A brand architecture in which the corporate name stays off the products and each brand carries its own separate equity — Procter & Gamble's Tide, Pampers and Gillette show no visible parent — which is the opposite of a branded house, where one master name fronts every offering; the trade-off is that a failure in one brand cannot contaminate the others, paid for by funding awareness separately for each name.
terms.whyItMatters: Corporate-branding roleplays ask whether a new line should carry the parent name; the answer turns on this architecture choice and the contamination risk it prices.

terms.definition: The channels ads run on — TV, radio, print, digital, outdoor, and social.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the right media reaches the target audience cost-effectively.

terms.definition: Technology that stores and manages employee data and HR processes.
terms.whyItMatters: An HRIS improves efficiency and enables data-driven HR decisions.

terms.definition: The initial stretch during which founder or employee equity is granted but not yet earned. On the standard four-year schedule nothing at all vests for the first twelve months, then 25% vests at once on the anniversary and the rest accrues monthly — so a cofounder who leaves in month eleven departs with zero shares.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay about a cofounder walking out early turns on this clause; without it the departing founder keeps a large stake and the venture becomes unfundable, which is the consequence a judge wants named.

terms.definition: The structured steps that move a customer from awareness to purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the process helps competitors execute each stage well.

terms.definition: The Consumer Product Safety Act duty to notify the Commission within 24 hours of obtaining information that a product contains a defect creating a substantial hazard, fails a mandatory standard, or poses an unreasonable risk -- and the duty applies even when the firm still disputes the defect.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics and consumer-protection roleplays test whether you report before finishing your own investigation; waiting for certainty is the answer that loses the indicator and, in practice, draws the fine.

terms.definition: Divides a market by activities, interests, opinions, values and lifestyle captured through AIO inventories, unlike demographic segmentation, which uses census-verifiable facts such as age, income and household size; two 34-year-olds each earning $60,000 fall in one demographic cell and can still land in opposite psychographic segments, which is why demographics alone cannot explain why one buys the premium line.
terms.whyItMatters: A market-planning roleplay that hands you a customer base and asks for a segmentation base is scored on naming the base and defending it against the other three; the usual failure is calling lifestyle data 'demographics'.

terms.definition: Media cost divided by impressions delivered and multiplied by 1,000 — a $6,000 magazine page reaching 400,000 readers is $15 — the conversion that makes a cheap small vehicle and an expensive large one directly comparable.
terms.whyItMatters: The most common media-math item on the marketing exam gives two vehicles with different prices and different audiences and asks which is the better buy; the raw price answers nothing and this figure answers it in one step.

terms.definition: The right of a worker leaving an employer with 20 or more employees to keep the group health plan for up to 18 months, extended to 29 months for disability and 36 months for a spouse or dependent after divorce or death. The qualified beneficiary has 60 days to elect and may be charged 102% of the full premium — the employer subsidy ends, which is why the monthly cost often quadruples.
terms.whyItMatters: A separation roleplay is scored on stating the election window and that the former employee now pays the full premium plus the 2% administrative charge.

terms.definition: Shares set aside for future hires, usually 10% to 20% of the company. Investors normally insist the pool be carved out of the pre-money valuation, which means the whole dilution lands on the existing shareholders — a 15% pool inside an $8 million pre-money quietly lowers the price the founders are really being paid.
terms.whyItMatters: In a term-negotiation roleplay this is the term that changes the effective valuation without changing the headline number; a competitor who negotiates only the valuation and ignores where the pool sits has conceded the point.

terms.definition: Selling price minus variable cost per unit - the dollars each extra sale releases to cover fixed costs and then profit. Gross profit per unit subtracts the full cost of goods sold instead, charging the unit for fixed manufacturing cost that this measure deliberately leaves out.
terms.whyItMatters: Every break-even item on the finance exam needs this figure first, and a competitor who reaches for gross profit computes a break-even volume that is too high.

terms.definition: Nothing can be inspected, weighed, or returned before purchase, so buyers judge search qualities beforehand, experience qualities only during delivery, and credence qualities -- a surgeon's technique, a tax opinion -- never at all; a good lets buyers verify most attributes before paying.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay contrasting service marketing with product marketing is scored on the tangible cues you add -- uniforms, facilities, guarantees -- to stand in for inspection.

terms.definition: A brand architecture where one master name fronts every offering and the sub-offerings are descriptors rather than brands — Google Maps, Google Drive, FedEx Freight — so every dollar of marketing on any one product raises awareness for all of them; the opposing structure is a house of brands, where each product owns its equity and one scandal is quarantined to a single name instead of reaching the whole portfolio.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay weighing a launch's branding cost against its risk is decided by naming both architectures and the efficiency-versus-contagion trade between them.

terms.definition: What one rating point of a market costs: spot price divided by the program's rating, so a $3,000 spot on a 5-rated program is $600. It prices a percentage of a market where cost per thousand prices raw impressions, which is why it cannot be compared across markets of different sizes.
terms.whyItMatters: Broadcast-buying items ask a competitor to rank stations within one market, where this is the right measure, then ask to compare a small market against a large one, where it is the wrong one and cost per thousand is needed instead.

terms.definition: The Affordable Care Act rule that an employer averaging 50 or more full-time-equivalent employees in the prior year must offer minimum essential coverage to at least 95% of full-time employees and their dependents or owe a per-employee penalty. Full time here means 30 hours a week or 130 a month, and coverage is affordable only if the employee's share of self-only premium stays under roughly 9.5% of household income as annually indexed.
terms.whyItMatters: A growing-business roleplay that asks whether hiring the 50th worker changes obligations depends on the FTE count and the 30-hour line, not on the payroll headcount.

terms.definition: Raising capital from a large number of small investors who each receive real shares and an ownership claim, which makes the raise a securities offering subject to filing and reporting. Rewards crowdfunding sells a pre-order or a perk instead, creates no shareholder, and triggers no securities filing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay comparing two online raises is graded on this split: one leaves the founder with hundreds of shareholders on the cap table forever, the other leaves only orders to fulfill.

terms.definition: A structured walk through every way a process step can fail, scoring each on severity, likelihood of occurrence and likelihood of detection from 1 to 10 and multiplying the three into a risk priority number as high as 1,000, so limited engineering time goes to the highest-scoring failure modes first.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations and quality roleplays reward a named method for choosing which defect to fix first; the priority number gives the judge an auditable reason for your order.

terms.definition: A label a written warranty may carry only if it repairs defects free within a reasonable time, puts no duty on the buyer beyond giving notice, does not limit the duration of implied warranties, and offers a refund or replacement after a reasonable number of failed repairs; missing any one forces the 'limited' label.
terms.whyItMatters: Warranty roleplays ask what a store may print on the tag; a written warranty that charges a handling fee cannot be called full, and knowing which of the four conditions broke is the scoring point.

terms.definition: A product brand that leads with its own name while carrying a visible parent guarantee — Courtyard by Marriott, Polo by Ralph Lauren — sitting between a house of brands, where no parent is shown at all, and a sub-brand, where the parent name leads and the descriptor trails, as in Microsoft Office; the endorsement lends credibility without forcing the parent to own the product's positioning.
terms.whyItMatters: Hotel and hospitality roleplays about launching a new tier are answered with this middle structure, and judges expect the sub-brand contrast to be drawn explicitly.

terms.definition: Targeted messages sent straight to individuals by mail, email, or phone.
terms.whyItMatters: Direct marketing allows personalized, measurable, one-to-one engagement.

terms.definition: Offers accepted divided by offers extended, times 100 — 27 acceptances on 36 offers is 75%. Declines by candidates who never received a formal offer are excluded, so the figure isolates whether pay and the closing conversation are competitive, not whether sourcing produced enough applicants.
terms.whyItMatters: In a compensation roleplay, a falling acceptance rate is the evidence that a pay range lags the market; the judge wants the ratio, not an impression that candidates seem unhappy.

terms.definition: A loan made by an ordinary bank that the Small Business Administration guarantees against default — 85% of the balance on loans up to $150,000 and 75% above that, to a $5 million ceiling. The guarantee is what persuades a lender to accept a borrower whose collateral and operating history would otherwise be too thin.
terms.whyItMatters: In a financing roleplay for a start-up that a bank has already declined, naming this program and the guarantee percentage is the concrete recommendation a judge is waiting for.

terms.definition: Vests copyright in the employer or commissioning party at the moment of creation instead of in the person who made the work, and it arises exactly two ways: a work prepared by an employee within the scope of employment, or a specially commissioned work that falls into one of nine statutory categories and is covered by a signed written agreement. Anything else a freelancer creates stays theirs until assigned in writing.
terms.whyItMatters: A startup roleplay about who owns the logo a contract designer drew is decided by whether a signed assignment ever existed.

terms.definition: Production and consumption happen at the same instant with the buyer present, so the employee is part of the product and no defective unit can be caught before a customer receives it; a manufactured good is built, inspected, and warehoused weeks before anyone buys it.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-quality roleplays are scored on front-line hiring and training as quality control, because there is no inspection step to add between production and the customer.

terms.definition: Groups buyers by what they measurably did — purchase occasion, usage rate, loyalty status, benefit sought — read from transaction records, while psychographic segmentation groups them by what they say they value and geographic segmentation by where they live; a heavy user and a light user can match on every demographic and psychographic trait and still belong in different behavioral segments, so it is the only base that predicts volume directly.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty-program roleplays ask which customers to reward; the winning answer segments on measured usage rate rather than on who the customers are.

terms.definition: Total media spend divided by completed conversions rather than by clicks — $800 producing 16 purchases is $50, even though that same $800 buying 3,200 clicks made cost per click look like $0.25. Rising here with a flat cost per click means the landing page, not the media, is failing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item showing cheap clicks and expensive customers is testing whether the competitor can locate the failure downstream of the ad, and a roleplay client who wants to cut the ad budget is usually the one who needs the page fixed.

terms.definition: The mechanism that ties a state unemployment tax rate to an employer's own history of benefit charges — an employer that has laid off heavily may pay several times the rate of one that has not, on the same taxable wage base. Federal unemployment tax is 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each worker's wages, reduced by a 5.4% credit to a net 0.6%, or $42 per employee, when the state account is in good standing.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost questions about layoffs versus reduced hours turn on the rating consequence, which competitors usually miss by treating unemployment tax as a fixed cost.

terms.definition: The pre-contract document sketching a deal's outline, in which price and structure are expressly non-binding but the exclusivity, confidentiality and expense-allocation clauses bind the moment it is signed — so it is emphatically not the harmless handshake its informal tone suggests.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-sale roleplay where the seller wants to keep talking to another buyer turns on which clauses in this document survive; the judge is testing whether you know price is the part that does not bind.

terms.definition: The motion in Robert's Rules that closes debate and forces an immediate vote on the pending item. It is not the item itself and it is not a question: it must be seconded, is undebatable and unamendable, and takes a two-thirds vote because it strips members of the right to speak. Someone shouting 'Question!' from the floor has not made this motion and has not ended debate - the chair must still put it to the assembly.
terms.whyItMatters: A meeting-procedure item that shows a chair cutting off discussion on a simple majority is testing the two-thirds threshold attached to this motion.

terms.definition: The liability booked at the moment of sale for repairs expected later -- units sold times expected claim rate times cost per claim, so 100,000 units at a 2% claim rate and $40 per claim accrues $80,000 of expense in the period the revenue is recognized, not when the repairs happen.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions pairing a generous warranty with its cost are answered with this accrual; a roleplay proposing a longer warranty has to price it, and the reserve is the number to quote.

terms.definition: Launching into a different product category under an existing brand name — Dove soap into Dove shampoo — whereas a line extension adds a variant inside the category the brand already sells, such as another Dove soap scent; the category jump risks diluting what the parent name means, while the in-category variant mainly risks stealing volume from its own siblings, so the two carry different failure modes and different tests.
terms.whyItMatters: Product roleplays that hand you a growth mandate are scored on naming which of the two you chose and the specific risk it carries; treating them as the same move loses both points.

terms.definition: Customer recommendations and referrals that spread opinions about a product.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth builds organic advocacy and trust beyond paid ads.

terms.definition: A selection interview in which every candidate receives the same predetermined questions in the same order and answers are scored against written anchors, rather than the interviewer following the conversation wherever it goes. Research places its predictive validity near .51 against roughly .38 for the unstructured version, and the fixed script is also what makes the process defensible when a rejected applicant alleges disparate treatment.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring roleplay asking how to make interviews fairer is answered by fixing the question set and the scoring key, not by adding a second interviewer.

terms.definition: The 23-item filing a franchisor must place in a prospect's hands at least 14 calendar days before any money changes hands or any agreement is signed. Its items cover fees, litigation and bankruptcy history, territory rights, and the roster of current franchisees plus everyone who left in the past three years.
terms.whyItMatters: A franchise-purchase roleplay is scored on whether you use the waiting period to call former franchisees; a competitor who signs on the spot has skipped the protection the rule exists to give.

terms.definition: A privacy demand the business must first authenticate as coming from the consumer, then answer within 45 days, extendable once by a further 45 with notice, covering the categories collected in the preceding 12 months. It must be handled free of charge unless it is manifestly unfounded or excessive, and acting on it without verifying identity is itself a breach.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a caller demands their records deleted tests whether the competitor verifies identity before acting and can state the response clock.

terms.definition: Unused capacity is destroyed the moment it goes unsold: a 200-room hotel that sells 150 rooms tonight cannot add the other 50 to tomorrow's inventory, which is why capacity is priced by demand period; unsold physical goods simply stay in inventory and sell later.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about slow midweek nights are scored on demand-shifting tactics -- off-peak pricing, overbooking policy -- that follow directly from capacity that cannot be stored.

terms.definition: Share of respondents who name a brand when asked only to list the brands they can think of in a category with nothing shown to them, as opposed to aided awareness, where the interviewer reads the name and the respondent only confirms recognition; aided scores typically run two to four times higher than unaided ones, so the two measures can never be compared with each other or with a competitor's differently-worded question.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that hand you awareness research want you to challenge the number's basis before acting on it; treating an aided figure as proof of strong awareness is the standard trap.

terms.definition: Revenue attributable to a campaign divided by what that campaign cost: $40,000 of revenue on $10,000 of spend is 4.0. It differs from return on investment, which subtracts cost of goods and the spend itself before dividing, so a 4.0 here is still a losing campaign at a 20% gross margin.
terms.whyItMatters: A client presenting a campaign as a four-to-one success is the setup for this distinction; the competitor is expected to ask for the margin before agreeing the campaign made money.

terms.definition: Requires equal pay for men and women performing jobs of equal skill, effort and responsibility under similar working conditions in the same establishment, and unlike a Title VII claim it needs no proof of intent. An employer escapes liability only through one of four defenses — a seniority system, a merit system, a system measuring quantity or quality of production, or any factor other than sex — and may never correct a gap by lowering the higher-paid worker's wage.
terms.whyItMatters: A pay-audit roleplay is scored on naming a permitted defense for the differential rather than asserting that the two jobs simply have different titles.

terms.definition: The SEC exemption that lets a company raise up to $5 million in any twelve months from the general public through a registered funding portal, capping how much a non-accredited investor may put in based on their income and net worth, and obliging the issuer to file annual reports afterward.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a financing roleplay whether the venture can simply ask the public for money, the answer is yes but only inside this exemption — the ceiling and the ongoing reporting duty are the tested details.

terms.definition: The total market value of all final goods and services a country produces in a year.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP is the standard gauge of economic health competitors reference.

terms.definition: Defect count divided by units shipped, times 1,000,000: 35 rejects out of 500,000 units is 70, the scale supplier scorecards use because the same figure written as a percentage -- 0.007% -- rounds toward nothing and cannot separate a good supplier from an excellent one.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays hand you competing quality records; comparing them on this scale, rather than on a rounded percentage, is what makes the recommendation defensible.

terms.definition: Lost unit sales of a firm's existing products divided by the unit sales of the new product that displaced them — 30,000 new units alongside a 12,000-unit drop on the old line is a 40% rate, leaving 18,000 units of true incremental volume; a launch reported on gross volume alone can show growth while total company units fall, which is why the ratio is computed before the launch is called a success.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay presenting strong launch numbers usually hides this; asking for the effect on the existing line is what separates a scored answer from applause.

terms.definition: An ad's key elements — headline, copy, visuals, call to action, and branding.
terms.whyItMatters: Each component ensures the ad communicates its message persuasively.

terms.definition: Protects workers aged 40 and over at employers with 20 or more employees, so a 38-year-old passed over for a 55-year-old has no claim under it and neither does a 12-person shop. Unlike Title VII, it protects only the older side of the line, meaning favoring a 60-year-old over a 45-year-old is not unlawful even though both are inside the protected class.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring-decision roleplay that mentions a candidate's age needs the 40-and-over line and the 20-employee threshold before you can say whether the statute even applies.

terms.definition: Capital repaid as a fixed slice of monthly revenue — commonly 3% to 8% — until a set multiple of the advance, usually 1.3x to 1.5x, has been returned. There is no fixed maturity date the way a term loan has one, and no ownership is given up the way an equity round would require.
terms.whyItMatters: In a financing roleplay for a venture with steady revenue but no collateral, this is the recommendation that avoids both dilution and a fixed payment the slow months cannot cover.

terms.definition: The ability to understand and manage emotions in yourself and others.
terms.whyItMatters: It underlies teamwork, service, and conflict-resolution answers.

terms.definition: The share of units clearing a step with no rework or scrap; multiplied across steps it gives rolled throughput yield, so four stations each at 95% deliver only 0.95^4 = 81.5% clean units, meaning a line whose every station reports 95% is really losing almost one unit in five.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality roleplays are scored on catching hidden rework: each station passing its own target while the finished-goods number falls short is exactly the scenario this calculation explains.

terms.definition: Plots competing brands against two axes chosen from the attributes buyers actually use to tell brands apart — often price against perceived quality — using respondent ratings rather than the firm's own specifications, and adds an ideal point where the target segment says it wants a brand to sit; an empty region on the map is a positioning opportunity only when an ideal point falls inside it, otherwise it is empty because nobody wants that combination.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays that hand you competitor data are scored on naming the two axes and defending why buyers discriminate on them; competitors lose the point by mapping attributes only the company cares about.

terms.definition: An auction in which the winner pays one increment above the runner-up's bid rather than the amount they themselves bid, so a $4.00 bid beating a $2.50 bid clears at $2.51 — which is why bidding true value can never cost more than that value is worth.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-buying items ask why an advertiser should enter its real maximum instead of shading the bid down; the mechanic, not the strategy, is the answer, and competitors who guess pay-what-you-bid get it backwards.

terms.definition: An appraisal method that requires managers to sort employees into fixed proportions — often 20% top, 70% middle and 10% bottom — regardless of how the group actually performed, so a strong team must still produce a bottom 10%. Its counterpart, a behaviorally anchored rating scale, rates each person against written behavior standards with no quota, which is why the two produce different outcomes for the same identical team.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect the quota objection when a roleplay asks whether to adopt ranking: rating a high-performing department this way forces an unfair low rating.

terms.definition: A fixed-length cohort program, typically about three months and ending in a demo day, that invests roughly $100,000 to $150,000 in exchange for about 6% to 7% of the company. An incubator by contrast offers space, services and mentoring on an open-ended timeline and often takes no equity at all.
terms.whyItMatters: In a roleplay choosing between two support programs, the graded discriminator is the equity cost against the deadline: one buys a demo-day audience with dilution, the other buys time without it.

terms.definition: Federal law governing consumer credit files: it grants access to the report, sets who may pull it, and obliges a bureau to investigate a disputed item.
terms.whyItMatters: A client in a roleplay whose report shows an account they never opened has a statutory remedy under it, not just a complaint.

terms.definition: The same offering varies by employee, by customer, and by hour, so quality is a distribution rather than a specification; a factory good is held to a stated tolerance and any unit outside it is scrapped, while service variance has to be squeezed by scripts, training, and blueprints.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on internal service standards is scored on how you narrow the spread between your best and worst shift, not on restating that people differ.

terms.definition: Two independently known brands appear together on one finished offering and both stake positioning risk on it — a Doritos Locos Taco — whereas in ingredient branding one brand is a component inside a host product and is advertised to end users to pull the host's sales, as with Intel Inside; the ingredient brand never owns the final purchase decision, while co-brands share it and share the damage if the partner stumbles.
terms.whyItMatters: Partnership roleplays ask what each side actually contributes and risks; naming which of the two structures is on the table is the first thing the judge listens for.

terms.definition: Coordinating all promotion for one consistent message across channels.
terms.whyItMatters: Consistency across touchpoints reinforces the message and maximizes impact.

terms.definition: Sets the conditions under which a worker 40 or older can validly waive an age claim in exchange for severance: at least 21 days to consider the agreement, a 7-day period to revoke after signing, written advice to consult an attorney, and consideration beyond what was already owed. In a group layoff the consideration period stretches to 45 days and the employer must disclose the job titles and ages of everyone selected and everyone spared.
terms.whyItMatters: Drafting a severance offer in a downsizing roleplay is incomplete without the review and revocation periods, and the group-layoff disclosure is the detail judges reward.

terms.definition: A venture deliberately held at the size that supports its owner's income and preferred schedule, funded out of its own cash flow and valued on owner earnings when sold. A scalable startup instead accepts deep planned losses to chase a market big enough to return an investor's entire fund.
terms.whyItMatters: A judge who asks whether to take outside investment is testing this choice: the venture that never intends to exit should not sell equity, because the investor's return depends on a sale that will never come.

terms.definition: Copies only the blocks changed since the previous backup of any type, so each nightly run is the smallest possible, but restoring requires the last full backup plus every one of these runs applied in order since it — and a single missing or corrupt link breaks the entire chain behind it.
terms.whyItMatters: Records-storage items ask why a company whose nightly job finishes in four minutes still needed nine hours to recover, and the restore chain is the reason.

terms.definition: Sorts features into must-be, whose absence angers buyers while its presence earns nothing, performance features, where satisfaction rises with the amount delivered, and delighters, unnoticed when missing but thrilling when present -- and it predicts each delighter decays into a must-be as rivals copy it.
terms.whyItMatters: Feature-prioritization roleplays are scored on where to spend: pouring money into a must-be buys no preference, while the delighter that differentiates today becomes table stakes next season.

terms.definition: Weakening of a famous mark's distinctiveness through blurring, where an unrelated use erodes the one-to-one link between mark and source, or tarnishment, where a use ties it to something unsavory; under the U.S. Trademark Dilution Revision Act of 2006 the owner of a mark famous to the general consuming public can sue without showing any likelihood of confusion or proof of actual economic injury, which is what makes it broader than ordinary infringement.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding and business-law roleplays about a licensing or extension request turn on this doctrine; citing the no-confusion-required standard is the technical half of the answer.

terms.definition: The Media Rating Council standard that counts a display impression only when at least 50% of its pixels hold the screen for one continuous second — two continuous seconds for video — so a campaign can serve 1,000,000 impressions and have only 600,000 of them count.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay where the client is billed for impressions the audience never had a chance to see is resolved by this standard, and exam items use the gap between served and counted impressions to test whether the competitor knows the threshold.

terms.definition: A documented escalation applied to correctable conduct — typically verbal warning, written warning, final written warning or suspension, then termination — with each step recorded, dated and acknowledged so the record shows notice was given. It is deliberately bypassed for gross misconduct such as theft, violence or safety sabotage, where immediate termination is appropriate, and skipping steps for ordinary conduct is what makes a later discharge look pretextual.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervisor roleplay about a chronically late employee is scored on naming the step reached and what documentation exists, not on describing a conversation.

terms.definition: Ownership issued for labor rather than cash, valued at what buying that work would have cost. Because the shares are normally restricted and vest over time, the recipient has 30 days from the grant to file an 83(b) election and be taxed on today's near-zero value instead of on the higher value at each future vesting date.
