terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay about paying an early developer in shares is scored on whether you flag the filing window; missing it hands the recipient a tax bill on paper gains they cannot sell.

terms.definition: Charting sample measurements over time against limits computed from the process's own variation to separate common-cause noise from assignable-cause shifts; it monitors a process while it runs, unlike acceptance sampling, which judges a finished lot after the fact.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality-method roleplays ask how to catch a drifting machine before it produces scrap; watching the charted trend is the in-process answer, and inspecting finished goods is the one judges mark as too late.

terms.definition: A process map drawn in horizontal bands split by the line of interaction, the line of visibility, and the line of internal interaction, so front-stage steps the customer sees sit above the backstage support that produces them, with failure points and wait times marked on the flow.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations roleplays that ask you to redesign a guest experience are scored on separating what the customer sees from the support behind it, which is where most delays actually live.

terms.definition: A one-sentence internal formula built from four required elements — the target segment, the frame of reference (the category the brand is to be compared against), the point of difference, and the reason to believe that substantiates it; drop the frame of reference and the claim has no competitive set to be better than, drop the reason to believe and it is an assertion. It is never customer-facing copy, which is the tagline's job.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges frequently ask a competitor to state the positioning out loud; delivering all four elements in one sentence is the difference between a scored answer and a slogan.

terms.definition: Marketing through online channels such as social media, email, and search.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital promotion reaches audiences efficiently with measurable results.

terms.term: Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA)
terms.definition: Guarantees reemployment to a worker returning from military service, capped at five years of cumulative absence from one employer, with the return application due within 1 day for service under 31 days, 14 days for service of 31 to 180 days, and 90 days beyond that. The escalator principle puts the returning worker in the position they would have reached had they never left, not merely the job they held on departure.
terms.whyItMatters: A reinstatement roleplay is scored on the escalator principle — offering the old job back at the old pay is the wrong answer when promotions occurred meanwhile.

terms.definition: The shape a venture's cumulative cash flow traces over time — falling deeper into negative territory through product build and customer acquisition, bottoming at the point of maximum funding need, then climbing as retained customers pay back. The depth of that trough, not the eventual slope, determines how much must be raised.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a planning roleplay why a growing, profitable-per-customer venture still runs out of money, this curve is the explanation, and the trough is the number the raise has to cover.

terms.definition: Renewal credit a credentialed professional must earn on a fixed cycle to keep the credential active — most state boards require a CPA to report 120 hours across a rolling three-year period with a 20-hour annual floor plus a mandated ethics course, and unused hours lapse rather than carry forward. Unlike a degree, it has no completion point.
terms.whyItMatters: The finance roleplay that asks how an accountant stays qualified year to year wants the cycle and the hour count, not a sentence about lifelong learning.

terms.definition: The matrix that converts weighted customer wants into engineering specifications, scoring each intersection 9, 3, or 1 for a strong, moderate, or weak relationship, then ranking every specification by the sum of customer weight times relationship score to decide what engineering works on first.
terms.whyItMatters: A product-development roleplay that must justify which feature ships first is scored on tracing the choice back to weighted customer input rather than to engineering preference.

terms.definition: Values a brand as the licensing fee the owner avoids paying by owning it: forecast the revenue the brand will carry, multiply by an arm's-length royalty rate drawn from comparable licenses — commonly 2% to 6% of net sales — deduct tax, then discount the resulting stream to present value; unlike a cost-based valuation it ignores what was actually spent building the name, and unlike a market comparison it needs no sale of a similar brand.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking what the brand is worth on the balance sheet expects a named valuation method with its arithmetic, not the claim that a brand cannot be valued.

terms.definition: Clicks divided by impressions: 250 clicks on 125,000 impressions is 0.2%, which is an ordinary display result and a poor search result. The denominator is impressions served, not people reached, so the figure falls as frequency rises even when the creative is working.
terms.whyItMatters: Campaign-review roleplays hand over a rate that dropped week over week; the competitor is expected to check whether frequency rose before concluding the creative went stale.

terms.definition: The employment eligibility verification record required of every U.S. employer by the Immigration Reform and Control Act: the employee completes Section 1 no later than the first day of work for pay, and the employer examines original documents and completes Section 2 within three business days of that start. The form is retained three years after hire or one year after termination, whichever is later, and is kept apart from the personnel file.
terms.whyItMatters: An onboarding roleplay that lists paperwork must place this inside the three-business-day window, a deadline competitors routinely confuse with the first payroll run.

terms.definition: A sale structured so the buyer takes only the assets it names and only the liabilities it lists, leaving unknown claims behind with the seller's legal entity and resetting depreciation on what was bought. A stock purchase transfers the whole company instead — contracts and licenses intact, but hidden liabilities included.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in an acquisition roleplay which structure to recommend, the buyer's answer and the seller's answer differ for a reason you must be able to state: liability follows the entity in one structure and not the other.

terms.definition: A growth grid crossing products (existing vs. new) with markets (existing vs. new) to produce four moves — market penetration, market development, product development, and diversification — ordered from lowest to highest risk because each new axis adds unfamiliar variables.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks how a regional chain should grow next year is answered by naming the specific Ansoff cell and its risk level, not by saying 'expand'.

terms.definition: The element of a brand that is recognized but cannot be spoken -- a symbol, distinctive lettering, color, or design -- as against the brand name, which is the part said aloud, and the trade name, which identifies the company rather than any product it sells.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand-building roleplays are scored on naming the pieces separately, since a logo redesign and a name change are different decisions with different legal and equity consequences.

terms.definition: Three decisions taken strictly in order — segment the market on one chosen base, target the segments worth serving against a stated attractiveness test, then position the offer against a named competitive set — where each step's output constrains the next; a positioning claim written before the segment is chosen has nobody in particular to be different for, which is why reordering the letters produces a plan that cannot be defended.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan roleplays are graded on sequence as much as content; presenting a promotion idea before naming the segment invites the judge to ask who it is for.

terms.definition: The specific group a promotional message is designed to reach.
terms.whyItMatters: Defining the audience shapes the message, media, and timing.

terms.definition: A structured conversation held with a current, valued employee while there is still time to act, asking what would make them leave and what keeps them — the findings can change that person's situation. An exit interview asks similar questions after the resignation is submitted, so its value is only aggregate trend data for future employees; the timing is the whole difference between the two.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that proposes only exit interviews concedes every departure; judges look for the forward-looking conversation with people still on the payroll.

terms.definition: Pricing a company at earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization multiplied by a factor taken from comparable completed sales: $800,000 of EBITDA at a 5x multiple gives a $4 million enterprise value, from which outstanding debt is subtracted and cash added back to reach the equity price.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-sale roleplay hands you an earnings figure and an industry multiple and asks what the owner walks away with; the debt subtraction is the step competitors skip.

terms.definition: A recurring fee the franchisee owes on GROSS SALES, not profit — commonly 4 to 8 percent — plus a separate advertising-fund contribution of about 1 to 3 percent, both paid on top of a one-time initial fee. Because the base is revenue, the fee is owed in full in a month the outlet loses money, which is the fact most competitors miss.
terms.whyItMatters: Franchise roleplays that ask whether a location can carry its costs are scored on running the royalty off sales; treating it as a share of profit produces the wrong break-even every time.

terms.definition: A standard states the minimum a unit must meet to be sold under a name at all, while a grade ranks the units that already clear it -- USDA beef sorted Prime, Choice, or Select by marbling and maturity has met one identical wholesomeness standard at every grade.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying and menu roleplays are scored on specifying the grade you will purchase; saying a product 'meets standards' says nothing about the quality tier you promised the customer.

terms.definition: The overall look and feel of a product or its packaging — the contour of a Coca-Cola bottle, a restaurant chain's interior scheme — protected under Lanham Act section 43(a) only when it is non-functional and has acquired secondary meaning in buyers' minds; product design trade dress can never be inherently distinctive, so unlike a coined word mark it always requires evidence that consumers link the look to a single source.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a competitor copying a store's look are scored on naming this protection and its two conditions; calling it a trademark or a copyright is the common miss.

terms.definition: Completed goal actions divided by the visits or clicks that could have completed them — the denominator is sessions, never impressions — so 40 orders from 2,000 landing-page visits is 2% no matter how many people saw the ad that sent them.
terms.whyItMatters: The single most common analytics error on the marketing exam is dividing sales by impressions; an item that supplies impressions, clicks and orders together is checking which denominator the competitor reaches for.

terms.definition: The deadline for bringing a federal discrimination charge — 180 calendar days from the discriminatory act, extended to 300 days in a deferral state that has its own fair employment agency covering the same conduct. Filing the charge is a prerequisite to suit, and once the agency issues a right-to-sue notice the employee has 90 days to file in court, a separate and much shorter clock.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint-handling roleplays test whether you know an internal investigation does not pause the statutory clock, and the 180/300-day split is the point being probed.

terms.definition: Asks whether the venture's current revenue growth would carry it to profitability before its cash runs out, holding spending flat from today. A venture that fails the test is default dead and must repair growth or cut costs now, rather than planning around a future round that may never be offered.
terms.whyItMatters: In a roleplay advising a founder who assumes the next investor will arrive, applying this test converts a hopeful plan into a dated decision about hiring and spending.

terms.definition: The smoothed yearly rate that carries a starting value to an ending value over n years: (ending value / beginning value)^(1/n) - 1. It deliberately hides year-to-year swings, so a category that jumped 40% and then fell 20% still reports one steady rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan questions that give a market size for two years and a span expect this exponent, not the two values subtracted and divided by the number of years.

terms.definition: Loss of trademark rights when the public adopts a mark as the common name for the whole product class -- aspirin, escalator, thermos; the Lanham Act's Section 14(3) test is the mark's primary significance to the relevant public, so an owner's protests do not save it once ordinary usage has flipped.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays about protecting a name are scored on naming the concrete defenses -- always pairing the mark with the generic noun, policing verb use -- and on why success itself creates the risk.

terms.definition: Incremental gross profit from a campaign minus its marketing cost, divided by that marketing cost: $150,000 of incremental revenue at a 40% gross margin against $30,000 of spend is ($60,000 - $30,000) / $30,000, or 100%. It runs on margin rather than revenue, and only on the lift a holdout group shows the campaign actually caused, so a campaign whose sales would have happened anyway returns a negative figure no matter how large the revenue number looks.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks whether a promotion paid for itself, the graded answer is this ratio on margin with a baseline, not the raw sales the campaign period produced.

terms.definition: Government and industry rules governing ad claims, content, and disclosure.
terms.whyItMatters: Compliance protects consumers and shields a business from liability.

terms.definition: The degree of discretionary effort and psychological commitment a worker brings to the organization's goals, measured through driver surveys covering manager quality, recognition and growth. It is not job satisfaction: a comfortable employee can be entirely satisfied and contribute nothing extra, which is why engagement tracks against productivity and turnover while satisfaction alone often does not.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how to build stronger employer-employee relationships expects engagement drivers and a measurement plan rather than a morale-boosting event.

terms.definition: Selling unpaid customer invoices to a third party for an immediate advance of roughly 80% to 90% of face value, with a fee of about 1% to 4% per 30 days deducted from the balance when the customer finally pays. A 2% fee on 30-day paper works out near a 24% annual cost, far above what the headline percentage suggests.
terms.whyItMatters: A cash-flow roleplay where a venture has sales on 60-day terms and payroll due Friday is answered with this tool; converting the fee to an annual rate is what shows the judge you understand its real price.

terms.definition: Deals won divided only by the deals that reached a final decision — wins plus losses — so 15 wins among 45 resolved deals is 33%, with open and no-decision opportunities excluded from the denominator entirely. That narrower denominator is the whole difference from close rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that hand you a pipeline table expect you to notice which opportunities belong in the denominator; counting still-open deals as losses is the single most common wrong answer.

terms.definition: Planning, developing, marketing, and managing offerings across their life.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures offerings meet customer needs and generate sustainable revenue.

terms.definition: Merchandise sold under the retailer's own name and sourced from a contract manufacturer, typically carrying a retail gross margin about 10 percentage points above the comparable national brand — roughly 35% against 25% — while retailing 15% to 30% cheaper, because the retailer carries no national advertising cost; the national brand by contrast is owned, advertised and priced by the manufacturer, who keeps that margin.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays about shelf space are settled with this margin arithmetic, and a competitor who argues only that the store brand is cheaper has missed why the retailer prefers it.

terms.definition: A purchase credited to an ad that was served and seen but never clicked, counted only when it falls inside a fixed look-back window — commonly one day for display against 30 days for a click — which is why these totals overstate a campaign next to click-through conversions.
terms.whyItMatters: A results presentation where the platform's reported sales exceed the client's actual order count is this in action, and the competitor is expected to say which conversions were assumed rather than observed.

terms.definition: A narrow statutory defense allowing an employer to hire on the basis of sex, religion, national origin or age when that characteristic is reasonably necessary to the essence of the business — an actor's sex for a specific role, or a mandatory retirement age for airline pilots. It can never justify a race-based decision, and it differs from business necessity, which defends a neutral rule that happens to screen out a group, whereas this defends an openly stated preference.
terms.whyItMatters: In a staffing roleplay involving a customer preference for one sex, the tested answer is that customer preference is not a valid basis for this defense.

terms.definition: The slice of an acquisition price held back at closing and paid only if the acquired business reaches agreed revenue or profit targets afterward. It bridges a buyer and seller who cannot agree on what the business is worth, and it is why a headline sale price routinely overstates the cash a founder actually receives.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-sale roleplay quotes an impressive price; the graded insight is asking how much is contingent and who will control the operations that decide whether those targets are hit.

terms.definition: Stated as a share of the selling price rather than in dollars: (price - variable cost) / price, or total contribution / total sales. It converts a dollar sales target straight into profit, and it differs from a gross margin ratio because only genuinely variable costs are subtracted from revenue.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks how much additional revenue is needed to fund a $5,000 promotion is solved by dividing that spend by this ratio, not by the gross margin.

terms.definition: Counts how many separate product lines a company carries, never how many items sit inside them: a grocer running dairy, bakery, and frozen lines has a width of 3 even when those lines hold 400 items between them, while product mix depth counts the items within one line.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix-planning roleplay that asks how a retailer should expand expects width and depth reported as two different counts; answering with adjectives like 'broad' instead of a number loses the indicator.

terms.definition: The sum of the discounted lifetime values of a firm's current and future customers — the asset value of the customer base itself — which can rise while brand equity falls, as when a firm buys volume with deep discounts and wins customers who think less of the name each year; brand equity is the value held in what buyers believe about the mark, customer equity the value held in the relationships and their future cash.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked whether a discount-driven growth plan is healthy, the judged answer separates the two equities and says which one the plan is spending down.

terms.definition: A schedule that alternates concentrated bursts with hiatus periods carrying no advertising at all — eight weeks on, four weeks dark — which buys higher in-season frequency than a flat continuous weight, at the cost of awareness decay during the dark weeks.
terms.whyItMatters: Seasonal-business roleplays turn on choosing this over pulsing or continuity, and the competitor is expected to name the trade the client is making rather than simply calling the plan seasonal.

terms.definition: A contract term requiring bargaining-unit employees to join the union or pay fees as a condition of continued employment — a union shop allows a grace period of 30 days after hire, shortened to 7 days in construction. Section 14(b) of the Taft-Hartley Act lets a state outlaw such clauses entirely, which is what a right-to-work state does, leaving the union obligated to represent employees who pay nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A labor-relations roleplay set in a right-to-work state is scored on knowing the clause is unenforceable there while the duty of fair representation continues.

terms.definition: A lump sum repaid by withholding 10% to 20% of daily card sales until a factor rate — normally 1.2 to 1.5 times the amount advanced — has been satisfied. Because a factor rate is a flat multiple rather than an interest rate, a 1.3 factor repaid over six months costs vastly more per year than 30%.
terms.whyItMatters: An ethics-flavored financing roleplay asks whether to accept fast funding at this price; the graded move is converting the factor rate into an annual cost before answering.

terms.definition: A short pre-approved message released in the first hour of an incident that confirms only what is known, states what the organization is doing about it, and promises a further update at a named time — issued precisely because the facts are not yet established.
terms.whyItMatters: In a crisis roleplay the judge is timing your first public response; silence while you investigate is scored as a failure to communicate.

terms.definition: The stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline.
terms.whyItMatters: The stage a product is in drives its marketing, pricing, and distribution.

terms.definition: The share and cost lead a pioneer can lock in through buyer switching costs, scarce shelf space or spectrum, and a learning-curve cost position — but Golder and Tellis found market pioneers failed roughly 47% of the time and held about 10% share on average, while the fast follower entering after the category's standard settles skips the cost of educating the market and buys the pioneer's proof of demand for free.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about racing a competitor to launch expect both sides argued with evidence; asserting that being first always wins is the answer the data contradicts.

terms.definition: A randomly selected slice of the target deliberately shown no advertising, so campaign lift is the exposed group's conversion rate minus the withheld group's — if exposed converts at 3.2% and the holdout at 2.6%, only 0.6 points were caused by the campaign and the rest would have happened anyway.
terms.whyItMatters: A client convinced a campaign drove every sale in its window is the setup for this method, and a competitor who can propose withholding a control group is answering a measurement question that platform-reported totals cannot.

terms.definition: The set of unwritten mutual expectations between employer and worker — promotion prospects, schedule flexibility, job security, loyalty — that no signed document records but both sides act on. Breaching it, such as quietly ending remote work after implying it was permanent, damages trust and drives resignations even when nothing legally binding was broken.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay describes an angry workforce after a policy change that violated no written rule, this is the concept that names what actually went wrong.

terms.definition: Financing of up to $50,000 — the typical loan running closer to $13,000 — made not by a bank but by nonprofit intermediary lenders on terms of up to 72 months, aimed at ventures too small to interest a 7(a) lender and normally conditioned on the borrower completing business training.
terms.whyItMatters: In a start-up roleplay for a venture needing a few thousand dollars of equipment, this program is the right named answer; recommending a 7(a) loan for that amount shows the sizes are not understood.

terms.definition: Protection lasting indefinitely, but only while three conditions hold: the information draws independent economic value from not being generally known, it is not readily ascertainable by proper means, and the owner takes reasonable measures to keep it secret through NDAs, access limits and labeling. The Defend Trade Secrets Act of 2016 added a federal civil claim for misappropriation. The trade-off against a patent is disclosure — a patent publishes the invention for about twenty years of exclusivity, while lawful reverse engineering destroys a secret with no remedy.
terms.whyItMatters: IP roleplays comparing a beverage recipe to a bottling machine ask which protection fits, and reverse-engineering risk is the deciding fact.

terms.definition: Counts the individual items inside a single line -- sizes, flavors, formulations, models: a toothpaste line of 4 flavors in 3 tube sizes is 12 items deep, and adding a fifth flavor deepens the mix without widening it, because width counts lines alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a table of lines and items and ask for one number; students who add every item in the company report the length instead of the depth of the line asked about.

terms.definition: A brand's share of category advertising spend minus its share of category sales — 12% of spend against 8% of sales gives +4 points. Binet and Field's analysis of IPA effectiveness cases found roughly every 10 points of positive excess buys about half a point of annual market-share growth, so a brand that holds its budget flat while rivals raise theirs loses share on an unchanged budget because the metric is relative, not absolute.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget roleplays that propose holding advertising spend steady are answered with this relative measure, which shows why a flat budget is a cut in competitive terms.

terms.definition: Google Ads' 1-to-10 diagnostic combining expected clickthrough rate, ad relevance and landing-page experience; it multiplies into the bid to set ad position, so an advertiser bidding $2.00 with a score of 8 outranks one bidding $3.00 with a score of 4 and pays less per click.
terms.whyItMatters: A search-advertising roleplay where the client wants to win position by raising the bid is the classic misread; the cheaper fix is tightening ad-to-keyword-to-page relevance, and the exam tests all three components by name.

terms.definition: Conduct prohibited by the National Labor Relations Act — Section 8(a) lists the five employer violations including interference with organizing, domination of a labor organization, discrimination for union activity and refusal to bargain in good faith, while Section 8(b) lists the union counterparts such as coercion of employees and secondary boycotts. A charge must reach the Board within six months of the conduct under Section 10(b).
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect you to identify which subsection a supervisor's threat falls under during an organizing-campaign roleplay, not merely to call the behavior unfair.

terms.definition: Identifying unmet market needs or underserved customer segments.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges assess how well competitors spot a genuine market need.

terms.definition: A member's assertion that the rules are being broken at this moment - a motion made out of order, debate wandering off the pending question, a vote miscounted. It may interrupt a speaker, requires no second, is not debatable, and is settled by the chair's ruling rather than a vote, though any two members may appeal that ruling to the assembly. It must be timely: raised after the offending action is complete, it is normally too late.
terms.whyItMatters: Chapter meetings and management roleplays run on a written agenda test whether you know which objections may interrupt a speaker and which must wait for the floor.

terms.definition: A group of related products sold under one brand or category.
terms.whyItMatters: Line decisions balance customer choice against cost and complexity.

terms.definition: Ehrenberg's empirical finding that a brand with a smaller customer base is punished twice over — fewer people buy it at all, and those who do buy it less often — so measured loyalty is almost entirely a consequence of penetration rather than an independent lever; the practical consequence is that a small brand's plan to grow purely by deepening loyalty among existing buyers contradicts the pattern found in essentially every category studied.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a retention-only growth plan for a small brand is a trap; naming this regularity and redirecting toward penetration is the scored move.

terms.definition: Total spend divided by clicks received — $800 over 3,200 clicks is $0.25 — a pricing basis that charges only when someone acts, unlike cost per thousand, which charges for the impression whether or not anyone ever clicks it.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay asks which pricing model protects a small client's budget; the answer turns on whether the goal is awareness, where impressions are the product, or traffic, where only the click is worth paying for.

terms.definition: The stepped route a complaint travels under a collective bargaining agreement — usually the immediate supervisor, then department management with a union steward, then a company-wide review, ending in binding arbitration by a neutral third party whose decision both sides accepted in advance. Each step carries its own filing deadline, and missing one can forfeit the claim regardless of merit.
terms.whyItMatters: A union-workplace roleplay is scored on routing the complaint through the contract's steps rather than settling it informally with the employee.

terms.definition: A hybrid structure combining corporate liability protection with partnership flexibility.
terms.whyItMatters: An LLC suits small ventures wanting protection without complex governance.

terms.definition: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's implementing rule, a consumer has 60 days from the statement showing a disputed debit-card or ACH transfer to notify the bank; the bank then has 10 business days to investigate, or may extend to 45 calendar days only if it posts provisional credit inside those 10 days, and must report its findings within 3 business days of finishing. Liability for a lost card is capped at $50 when reported within 2 business days of discovery and $500 after that. Credit-card charges are excluded — those run on the Fair Credit Billing Act's two-billing-cycle track.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services or banking roleplay in which a client's debit card was drained overnight is scored on whether the competitor cites the 10-business-day investigation and the provisional-credit condition, instead of promising an immediate refund no associate can authorize.

terms.definition: Total number of items across every line the firm sells, equal to width multiplied by average depth: 5 lines averaging 8 items each gives a length of 40, so a company can lengthen its mix without widening it by adding items to lines it already runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Product-mix questions hand you width and average depth and expect the multiplication; a roleplay judge scoring a merchandising plan looks for the total item count you commit the buyer to carrying.

terms.definition: A comprehensive, systematic, independent and periodic examination of a firm's whole marketing environment, objectives, strategies and activities — all four adjectives are required, so a review of one campaign conducted by the team that ran it qualifies as none of them; its deliverable is a ranked list of corrective actions, not a score or a performance rating.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks how you would diagnose a marketing department that is missing its targets, the independence and scope conditions are what distinguish an audit from an internal post-mortem.

terms.definition: Opens divided by messages delivered — not messages sent — so 4,000 opens on 20,000 delivered is 20% while the same 4,000 against 25,000 sent looks like 16%. The count only fires when a tracking pixel loads, so image blocking and Apple's Mail Privacy Protection both distort it.
terms.whyItMatters: A direct-marketing roleplay reporting a suspiciously high figure after a privacy change is testing whether the competitor knows the metric is inferred from a pixel and will point to clicks as the reliable measure instead.

terms.definition: The secret-ballot vote that decides union representation: a petition requires authorization cards from at least 30% of the proposed bargaining unit, and certification follows a simple majority of ballots actually cast, not of the unit — 40 votes for out of 70 cast in a 100-person unit certifies the union. A valid election bars another for 12 months, and a resulting contract bars one for up to three years.
terms.whyItMatters: Organizing roleplays test the 30% showing of interest against the majority needed to win, a pair of numbers competitors frequently collapse into one.

terms.definition: An analysis of whether a business idea is achievable, viable, and sustainable.
terms.whyItMatters: It justifies recommendations and addresses resource constraints.

terms.definition: The complete record of a nation's transactions with the rest of the world — the current account of goods, services, income and transfers, plus the capital and financial accounts — which sums to zero by construction, since a current-account deficit is financed by an offsetting inflow of capital. The balance of trade is only the goods-and-services slice of the current account.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items ask what a persistent trade deficit implies; the correct answer follows the offsetting capital inflow rather than treating the deficit as unfunded loss.

terms.definition: Building a company's overall reputation and identity across its offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong corporate branding creates loyalty and justifies premium pricing.

terms.definition: Rogers' model dividing adopters over time into five fixed bands measured in standard deviations from the mean adoption date — innovators 2.5%, early adopters 13.5%, early majority 34%, late majority 34% and laggards 16% — so the opinion-leading early adopters are a narrow 13.5% band that must be won before the 34% early majority will move, and a launch plan aimed at the mass market from day one is aimed at people who are not yet buying.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product roleplays ask who to target first; naming the band and its percentage is what turns 'we'll target trendsetters' into a defensible answer.

terms.definition: Copies a publication actually distributes in an average issue, audited by the Alliance for Audited Media, as opposed to readership, which multiplies those copies by a pass-along factor of roughly 2 to 3 — so a 500,000-copy magazine can legitimately claim 1,200,000 readers.
terms.whyItMatters: Print-buying items give one vehicle's audited copies and a rival's claimed readers and ask which is the larger audience; the competitor has to convert both to the same basis before the cost-per-thousand comparison means anything.

terms.definition: A rating form whose points are each defined by a real example of observable behavior — a 5 might read greets every guest within thirty seconds while a 2 reads acknowledges guests only after they approach — built from critical incidents gathered from people who do the job. A plain graphic rating scale labels the same points only excellent through poor, which is why two managers can rate identical behavior differently on it.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay complains that appraisals are inconsistent between supervisors, the tested fix is anchoring each scale point in described behavior.

terms.definition: Gross burn counts every dollar of cash leaving the venture in a month; net burn subtracts the cash collected in the same month, so a startup spending $90,000 and collecting $40,000 posts a $90,000 gross figure and a $50,000 net figure — investors size a raise off the net one.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay judge who asks how long your funding lasts is testing whether you quote net rather than gross; the finance-side exam item pairs the two figures and asks which one divides into cash on hand.

terms.term: Goleman's four-domain model of emotional intelligence
terms.definition: Sorts emotional competence into four domains — self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship management — arranged as a 2x2 grid: the left column is personal competence (handling yourself), the right column is social competence (handling others), the top row is recognition and the bottom row is regulation. It is a mixed model of learnable workplace competencies, so it is assessed with a 360-degree rater inventory rather than with a right-answer test.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that lists four manager behaviors and asks which one is social awareness rather than relationship management is scored against this grid, and a management roleplay judge expects a candidate to name which domain a weakness sits in before proposing the fix.

terms.definition: Adds a new size, flavor, color, or form under an existing brand inside the category it already competes in; a brand extension instead carries that brand into a different category -- a cherry version of a cola is the first, a cola-branded snack chip is the second.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask you to grow a brand without new advertising weight; naming the wrong one of the pair gives away that you cannot tell same-category growth from category entry.

terms.definition: Any contact at which a buyer forms a judgment about a brand with no marketing message present to help — Procter & Gamble named the 3 to 7 seconds facing the shelf the first such moment and the first use of the product the second; the practical rule is that advertising spend cannot repair a touchpoint at which the customer has already decided against the brand.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about check-in or complaint handling are scored on identifying the exact contact that decides the guest's opinion and fixing that, not on adding promotion.

terms.definition: An email permanently rejected because the address does not exist or the domain is dead, as opposed to a soft bounce, which is a temporary failure such as a full mailbox or a server outage and gets retried; mailbox providers begin filtering a sender whose permanent-failure rate passes roughly 2%.
terms.whyItMatters: A client whose newsletter suddenly lands in spam usually has an unpurged list, and a direct-marketing roleplay expects the competitor to distinguish the two failure types before recommending list hygiene.
